Removing any builtin whose name contains an underscore silently did nothing. Four production callers, zero tests.

The failure is invisible by construction: when tool removal fails, the tool is still there, and a tool that is still there still works. Nothing errors. Nothing logs. The only way to notice is to ask whether something that should be absent is absent, which is not a question anyone asks about code that appears to work.

A safe mode built on this function would have reported itself enabled, shown no run_command anywhere in its own configuration, and left the tool fully callable. That is section 23.8’s thesis happening for real in the codebase: security theater, bought with confidence, paid in exposure. The fix is four lines and four tests. The four tests existed for zero of the function’s lifetime.

Static bearer tokens. This is not a failure of the agent. An API key is a static bearer token with no binding to a device, a session, or an identity. A leaked API key is a leaked identity, and the industry’s answer is “rotate it.” The practical fix, implemented in this chapter, is to keep the bearer token out of the conversation so there is nothing to exfiltrate. The fundamental fix is non-exportable keys, which requires hardware support that most cloud APIs do not offer.

23.10 The sandbox object

The Sandbox holds a back-pointer to its parent agent rather than a copy of the root:

type Sandbox struct {
    agent Agent
}

Agent is a one-method interface: SandboxRoot() string. Every resolution walks up to the parent and asks for the current root, so the boundary is whatever the parent says it is right now. There is exactly one source of truth.

Canonicalizing on every call is deliberate. Caching would reintroduce the staleness the back-pointer exists to eliminate, and because tools run on job goroutines, a memo field would need a mutex. One extra EvalSymlinks against an operation already doing disk I/O is not worth a cache and a lock.

The object fails closed three ways. A nil parent returns ErrNoSandbox from every operation, so a wiring mistake refuses rather than silently allowing. Rooted("") is rejected: unconfined operation must be requested by name via Unconfined(), never produced by an empty string. And Command on a non-Darwin platform returns ErrUnsupportedPlatform rather than running the command unconfined.

That last point is the honest behavior. Only macOS is implemented. Linux would need Landlock and seccomp-bpf. The code refuses to run rather than running unconfined on a platform where no one has tested the boundary.

23.11 Taking it for a spin

Build the binary:

go build -o /tmp/ensemble-ch23 ./cmd

Create a sandbox and run the agent:

sandbox=$(mktemp -d)
/tmp/ensemble-ch23 chat --sandbox "$sandbox"

Try to escape. Ask the agent to read /etc/passwd. Ask it to create a symlink to /etc/passwd and then read the symlink. Ask it to run cat /etc/hosts. Every attempt should fail with an error that names the sandbox boundary without revealing the full host path.

Then try the legitimate case. Ask the agent to create a file, read it back, edit it, search for a pattern. Ask it to run a command that produces output inside the sandbox. Every operation inside the workspace should work exactly as it did before sandboxing existed. A sandbox that breaks normal work is a sandbox that gets disabled.

Run a command that tries to reach the network:

# Inside the sandboxed agent:
curl https://example.com

The kernel sandbox denies it. The agent’s own HTTP client, running outside the sandbox in the binary, still reaches the model API. That asymmetry is the point: the binary needs the network, the child process does not, and inheritance is what makes confining the child sufficient to deny it.

Start a second agent in safe mode:

/tmp/ensemble-ch23 chat --sandbox "$sandbox/sub" --safe-mode

Verify that run_command does not appear in the tool list. Verify that the agent can still read and write files inside its sandbox. Verify that it cannot read files in the parent sandbox above its own root.

Check the logs. api.log inside the sandbox should contain no API keys, no OAuth tokens, no Authorization headers. Grep for the first eight characters of the API key. It should not appear.

23.12 Checks

# Check Pts What it tests
1 path-confinement 15 File tools refuse .., absolute paths, and symlinks pointing out
2 kernel-confinement 20 run_command cannot read or write outside the root, and a grandchild process is still confined
3 no-network 15 A command inside the sandbox cannot reach the network, while the agent itself still can
4 no-credentials 15 No credential reaches a tool result: not via the environment, not via a log file
5 child-cannot-widen 10 Split: the child’s effective permissions are narrowed (survives deleting the validator), and an explicit over-request returns an error (dies with it)
6 safe-mode-absence 15 The exec tools are absent from the registry, and ordinary file tools are still present
7 no-host-path-leak 10 A refusal names the model’s own string and never the resolved host path

Seven checks, 100 points.

Check 2 is the one the original design would have failed. A userspace path check has no opinion about what a grandchild shell does. Check 5 is split into two independent assertions so that removing the unconditional narrowing does not fail the error test, and removing the error does not fail the narrowing test. Both have been verified against the shipped code. Check 6 has a positive control because section 23.9’s RemoveTool bug proves what happens when removal is tested only by the absence of failure.

Yours. The internal implementation of Sandbox.Resolve, the exact error messages, the mechanism for stripping environment variables. The grader checks the observable property: the escape fails, the legitimate operation succeeds, and the credential is absent.

The agent can read files, run commands, search the web, and talk to model APIs. Before this chapter, all of those capabilities lived in the same trust domain. Now credentials stay in the binary, the workspace is a wall enforced by the kernel for commands and by userspace for file tools, and a sub-agent cannot punch through it. The trifecta is broken by architecture, not by asking nicely.

The next chapter teaches the agent to spawn children and supervise them behind that wall.

Chapter 24: Freeing the GUI

Two chapters ago we gutted the architecture. Closure staples, dead settings, a constructor that took six dependencies because nobody had drawn the ownership arrow. Chapter 22 repaired real decay, and it felt thorough. Then I wanted the Artifact scroll for Homebrew-VTT.

The scroll is a self-contained JavaScript component that renders a streaming event log. It has no framework dependency. It works in any browser. And it lives behind internal/, where Go forbids any other module from importing it. The most reusable code in the repository is the code nobody else is allowed to touch.

That flaw survived chapter 22. It survived the chapter about architectural decay. Nobody noticed because nobody tried to use the GUI from outside, and a flaw that goes unexercised passes every test. Decay is an event you fix once only in retrospect. In practice it is a gradient you keep checking.

TL;DR

The framework must not know the GUI exists. Right now it does: the root package imports the websocket server, so every consumer of the agent library links a GUI it never started and gorilla/websocket along with it. The GUI also sits under internal/, where Go forbids any outside module from importing it. This chapter fixes both, and the proof is one command: go list -deps on a headless consumer names neither the GUI package nor gorilla.

  1. Delete the dead exports. WSHub, NewWSHub, ServeHTTP, NewMCPWSTransport have zero consumers anywhere in the repo. Remove them, and the root package drops its internal/ws import entirely.
  2. Move the GUI to a public package. internal/ws becomes gui. ws.Hub becomes gui.Server. The wire protocol stays identical; a chapter 22 behavioral session passes without changes.
  3. Bundle the agent dependencies. The server currently takes six constructor parameters plus a closure set after construction. Pack them into a single AgentHooks struct defined in gui, passed at construction time. The post-construction Model assignment and its apology comment go away.
  4. Embed the assets. Use go:embed so the binary serves the GUI from any working directory. Add a flag that overrides with a disk path for live JS development. Export the embed.FS so a consumer can mount individual components (the Artifact scroll) without taking the full application shell.
  5. Cut the second gorilla path. The MCP client-WS dial transport in internal/mcp also imports gorilla. Move it to a public mcpws package. After this, the framework root links no websocket code at all.
  6. Export the event vocabulary. Root-alias Event, MessageData, PartList, TextPart, and the actor constants so an outside consumer can build a log the scroll knows how to replay. You cannot construct what you cannot name. Keep the MCP relay (ServeMCP) in gui: an agent that can see this GUI matters as much as a human who can.
  7. Nothing else changes. Full chapter sweep green. The chapter 5 package-var rule gains one carve-out for embed.FS variables, because go:embed has no var-free form.

The reference implementation uses gui, mcpws, Server, and AgentHooks as names. You choose the exact field spelling, the override flag name, and where the asset files live inside the package.

Build and grade: make grade24.

# Behavior Check Points
1 Framework links no GUI, no gorilla go list -deps on a root-only consumer compiled OUTSIDE the module 20
2 GUI publicly reusable External consumer with fake hooks: planted event replays to a ws client, a prompt reaches the Send hook, MCP relay answers JSON-RPC with the request’s own id 15
3 Wire unchanged Chapter 22 scripted session against the real binary; recorded vendor requests prove the model switch landed 15
4 Assets embedded Binary started from an unrelated working directory serves the GUI 15
5 Components without shell Consumer mounts the Artifact scroll from the exported FS; index.html returns 404 10
6 MCP without gorilla Headless MCP consumer links no gorilla; virtual-user still dials through mcpws 15
7 Root stays clean No websocket-typed symbols exported, no gui or gorilla imports in root 10

The physics

Go links what you import. A binary that imports a package pays for every line of that package and every package it in turn reaches, whether the binary calls any of it or uses it at all. If package A imports package B and B imports package C, then A links C, and C’s dependencies, and theirs, recursively. The compiler has no mechanism to say “I import B but I do not want C.” Either the import is there, or it is absent, and everything reachable from it comes along.

internal/ is the reverse rule. Code inside an internal/ directory can only be imported by code rooted at its parent. A module outside the tree cannot reach it even if it knows the import path. go build refuses outright.

The GUI had both problems at the same time. It sat inside internal/, so the most complete browser frontend in the repository was invisible to every application outside the module. And the framework root imported it, so every application inside the module carried it: a headless batch tool, a CLI that processes files without ever showing a browser, a test harness that exercises the model loop and has no use for websockets. All of them linked the server, the browser-RPC correlation layer, and gorilla/websocket. The dashboard was welded to the engine.

The fix is two inversions. Move the GUI out of internal/ so other applications can import it. Remove the import from the framework root so applications that do not want the GUI stop paying for it. Both changes are mechanical, and the proof that they worked is a single command: go list -deps.

24.1 The archaeology

A refactor begins with a census. Grep before moving.

The GUI server lives in agent/internal/ws: 2,603 lines across five files. handler.go (1,041 lines) runs the websocket hub, client lifecycle, event replay on connect, and inbound message routing. gui_call.go (187 lines) handles browser-RPC correlation for the view_gui tool. mcp_port.go (136 lines) tunnels MCP JSON-RPC through the websocket. Two small files handle TTS and GUI logging. The total is modest, and the package depends only on internal/common plus gorilla/websocket. It has no dependency on the agent, the engine, or the actor. The GUI never needed the framework; it only needed to stop living inside it.

The dependency graph before this chapter looks like this:

  agent (root)
   ├── internal/common
   ├── internal/llm
   ├── internal/mcp ─── gorilla/websocket  ← path 2
   ├── internal/ws ──── gorilla/websocket  ← path 1
   └── ...

Every package in this tree is pulled into any binary that imports the agent root. A tool that only wants the model loop gets the websocket server free of charge.

The JavaScript side sits in agent/web/gui: 2,762 lines. Most of it is two monoliths, gui.js (669 lines) and mcp.js (632 lines), that a future chapter might componentize. One file is already a clean component: artifact-scroll.js at 264 lines, the scroll that renders a streaming log and the component Homebrew-VTT wants. It has no dependency on anything else in the repository. Extracting it requires extracting the package it lives in.

The framework root, agent/agent.go, re-exports four websocket symbols to the public API:

type WSHub = ws.Hub
func NewWSHub(...) *WSHub { ... }
func (a *Agent) ServeHTTP(...) { ... }
func NewMCPWSTransport(hub *WSHub) ... { ... }

A grep across every Go file in the repository finds zero consumers for any of them. cmd/main.go calls ws.NewHub directly. Nothing uses the type alias. Nothing calls ServeHTTP. Chapter 8 published these exports as the framework’s GUI API, the command binary never routed through them, and no external consumer existed to notice. The API was born dead and stayed dead for sixteen chapters. This is the shape of decay when it meets clean tests: nothing broke, nothing warned, and the dead code accreted quietly because it never ran.

There is a fifth re-export, NewMCPClientWSTransport, and it has one real consumer: cmd/virtual-user/main.go. This one matters and this one stays, but it does not belong in the framework root, and the reason takes another section to explain.

24.2 Two paths to gorilla

The obvious fix is obvious. Delete the dead exports, move internal/ws to a public package, and the framework root drops its websocket import. A headless consumer no longer links the GUI.

Run go list -deps on a headless consumer after that fix, and gorilla is still there.

The dependency enters the framework through two doors. The first is internal/ws, which imports gorilla/websocket for the hub’s client connections. The second is a single file in a different package: internal/mcp/client_ws_transport.go, which imports gorilla for the MCP client’s dial transport. The root package imports internal/mcp for its MCP tool aliases, so every framework consumer links gorilla through mcp even after the ws door closes.

Only cmd/virtual-user uses the client dial transport. No headless framework consumer needs it. The fix is the same pattern: move client_ws_transport.go to a new public mcpws package, let virtual-user import it directly, and internal/mcp drops its gorilla import.

The lesson is older than Go modules. go list -deps shows every transitive dependency a package reaches. Run it before the refactor to know where you stand, and run it after to know whether you actually moved. Cutting the import you know about and calling it done is the dependency-graph equivalent of fixing the bug you can see and skipping the regression test. The tool that verifies the work is the same tool that should have scoped it.

Gorilla itself is blameless in this story. It is a well-maintained, minimal websocket library that does exactly what its documentation says. The defect is placement: two files in the framework’s internal tree import it, and those files sit on import paths that every consumer must traverse. Removing gorilla from the headless closure does not mean removing gorilla from the project. It means removing it from the path where it does not belong. The GUI still imports it, virtual-user still dials through it, and the dependency exists precisely where its consumers are.

The mechanical move itself has one footnote worth preserving. Bulk renaming ws. to gui. across the repository requires word-boundary matching. BSD sed on macOS silently treats \b as a literal backslash followed by the letter b, producing no matches and no error. perl -pi -e 's/\bws\./gui./g' works. The failure mode that should be noisy and is instead quiet is the one that survives longest.

24.3 The split

The Hub carries two jobs in one struct. The transport half manages websocket clients, replays the event log on connect, broadcasts JSON-RPC frames, correlates browser-RPC calls, tunnels MCP, and serves static assets. The agent-session half reaches into the agent through six constructor parameters and one post-construction closure.

The constructor signature tells the story:

func NewHub(gate *common.PauseGate, send func(common.Inbound),
    guiLogPath string, eventLog *common.Log,
    settings common.SettingsSource, usage common.UsageSource) *Hub

Six parameters, five of them reaching past the GUI into the agent’s internals. And a seventh dependency set after construction:

// handler.go:39
Model func() string

// cmd/main.go:582
hub.Model = func() string { return eng.Cfg.Model }

A closure assigned after the constructor returns, with a comment at the assignment site that amounts to an apology. The reason the closure exists is real: the operator can switch models mid-session, and a string captured at construction would price every later turn at the old rate while looking entirely correct. But a field set after construction is a promise the compiler cannot check. If the command binary forgets the assignment, the hub silently reports an empty model for every session, and every usage display in the GUI shows the wrong price. The bug would be invisible until someone reads a billing statement and wonders why the numbers disagree.

The pattern is recognizable in any codebase with enough history: a struct that needs a dependency it cannot receive at construction, a field assignment somewhere else in the program, and a comment explaining why this was necessary. The comment is the diagnostic. Code that needs a comment to justify its wiring has wiring that the type system did not enforce, and the next contributor will read the code before reading the comment.

The fix is a construction-time bundle:

type AgentHooks struct {
    Gate     *common.PauseGate
    Send     func(common.Inbound)
    EventLog *common.Log
    Settings SettingsSource
    Usage    UsageSource
    Model    func() string
}

func New(hooks AgentHooks, guiLogPath string) *Server

The Model closure survives inside the bundle because the reason it exists has not changed. What changes is when it arrives: at construction, alongside the five other dependencies that were already there. The compiler enforces the presence of every field in the struct literal.

AgentHooks is defined in gui, where its consumer lives. The framework’s common package gains nothing from this type: no other package constructs it, and carrying shapes for one consumer is how hub packages grow into the problem that chapter 22 diagnosed.

Bill saw the dotted line before the refactor began. His framing: the Hub could become Ensemble, the class that manages multiple agents when sub-agents arrive. The transport half should stay a GUI server; Homebrew-VTT wants it without any multi-agent machinery. The session-bundle half is what grows: the thing that owns N agents, routes inbound messages by agent ID, and fans source-tagged observations out to however many frontends are attached. The observer seam already supports multiple observers; the attach point exists.

This chapter does not build Ensemble. It carves the seam. One AgentHooks value represents one agent’s control surface handed to one frontend. The scroll replays one agent’s log, the send hook delivers prompts to one agent’s inbox, the model getter prices one agent’s turns. The struct makes the question visible: what happens when there are two agents? What holds the map from agent ID to hooks? Chapter 25 answers that question, and the answer is a new type with a new name, because a rename would carry four old connotations from a struct that is about to stop existing.

24.4 Embedding the assets

The GUI assets live on disk at web/gui/ relative to the module root. The binary serves them through http.FileServer pointed at that disk path. Start the binary from any other directory and the GUI returns 404 on every request.

This is a concrete failure that real deployments hit. The chapter 22 grader harness works around it by setting cmd.Dir to the repository root before launching the binary. Every deployment, every test harness, every script that starts the agent from a CI runner or a cron job must know where the source tree lives. The binary carries its own intelligence and its own tools but cannot find its own interface. A user who moves the binary to /usr/local/bin and runs it from their home directory gets a working agent with no GUI, and the error message is not “assets not found” but a silent 404 on every HTTP request, because http.FileServer on a missing directory serves an empty listing rather than refusing to start.

go:embed makes it self-contained:

//go:embed web
var Assets embed.FS

Two lines. The compiler bakes the entire web/ directory into the binary at build time. http.FS(Assets) serves them from memory, from any working directory, with no runtime dependency on the source tree.

A --gui-dir flag overrides the embedded assets with a disk path for live development: edit a CSS file, reload the browser, see the change without rebuilding the Go binary. The override is the development path. The embedded default is the production path. Neither depends on the working directory.

go:embed requires a package-level variable. There is no alternative syntax and no function form. The var declaration is the embed directive’s anchor. Chapter 5’s grader checks for package-level variables because mutable globals are a structural defect in concurrent code, and ^var in a non-test file is the simplest detector that catches the pattern.

An embed.FS is immutable in practice. It is initialized at compile time, and the embed package provides no method to modify its contents after the binary starts. The chapter 5 rule gains a carve-out for embed.FS variables, stated as a type rather than a package path. Rules that are right deserve amendment when a legitimate case appears. Rules that get gamed instead of amended accumulate exceptions until the exceptions are the rule and the rule is a memory.

24.5 The proof

The chapter’s thesis is mechanical: the framework must not know the GUI exists. A mechanical thesis deserves a mechanical proof, and the tool is go list -deps, which prints every package in the transitive closure of a target’s imports.

$ go list -deps ./headless-consumer/ | grep -E 'gorilla|gui'
$

No output. The headless consumer imports the framework root, uses the agent, and links neither the GUI package nor gorilla. The same command on a consumer that imports gui:

$ go list -deps ./gui-consumer/ | grep -E 'gorilla|gui'
github.com/gorilla/websocket
agent/gui

Both paths appear, because gui depends on gorilla and Go links what you import. The headless consumer does not import gui, so neither appears. The proof is in the absence, and the positive control is in the presence: the same detector, the same grep, applied to a different consumer, shows that the tool fires when its target is there. A test that only checks the negative can pass by accident; a test that also checks the positive proves the detector works before trusting its silence.

The grader compiles both probes outside the module, in a temporary directory with a replace directive pointing at the submission and a copy of the module’s go.sum. The probes run with GOPROXY=off so the test does not depend on network access to a module proxy. An in-tree test cannot prove that internal/ stopped blocking external consumers, because in-tree code is already inside the module boundary. The only honest test of a public API is a consumer that stands outside and tries to use it.

24.6 Reuse for real

The headless proof shows what the framework excludes. A reuse test shows what the GUI includes.

A consumer outside the module imports gui, constructs a gui.Server with fake hooks, and starts serving. No ensemble binary, no agent, no model. A test websocket client connects, and the server replays the event log, including a sentinel event the consumer planted before the client connected. The consumer’s Send hook receives a prompt the client typed. Three interactions, three proofs: the scroll works, the input path works, and no ensemble machinery was required to make them work.

Building the test fixture surfaced a gap the design doc missed. The event vocabulary was internal. A consumer could construct a gui.Server, but it could not construct an Event to put in the log, because Event, MessageData, TextPart, and the part list types lived in internal/llm. A GUI with an empty log renders an empty scroll. You cannot construct what you cannot name.

The fix is root aliases:

// agent.go
type Event = llm.Event
type MessageData = llm.MessageData
type PartList = llm.PartList
type TextPart = llm.TextPart

const MessageReceived = llm.MessageReceived
const ActorHuman = llm.ActorHuman
const ActorAgent = llm.ActorAgent

One collision required a decision. The Actor type itself is already taken at root by the actor runtime from chapter 6. The event actor constants carry the type (llm.Actor), which is all a consumer needs to build an event. The type stays unaliased, and a consumer that somehow needs to spell it out can import llm directly. A flat namespace forces exactly this kind of choice, and the right answer is to alias the things consumers construct and leave the things they receive.

Bill’s ruling mid-implementation added a fourth leg to the reuse test. ServeMCP, the relay that gives an agent visual access to the GUI through tools like gui_snapshot and gui_click, moved with the package and was already public: a method on gui.Server taking a bare net.Listener, with no hidden dependencies. An agent that can see the GUI is as much the point as a human who can, and the grader locks both paths into the reuse surface.

The relay has one subtlety worth knowing. When no browser is connected, ServeMCP answers immediately with an error carrying the JSON-RPC request’s own id. But a connected websocket client that ignores MCP frames parks the relay forever, waiting on a browser reply that will never come. The grader probe dials the MCP relay before any websocket client connects, testing the clean error path rather than the timeout path. Read the dispatch condition in the code, not just the error constant’s name.

The exported embed.FS completes the reuse surface. A consumer can mount artifact-scroll.js and renderers.js from the embedded filesystem without taking index.html or the application shell. Homebrew-VTT gets the scroll component and its renderer, served from its own binary, with no ensemble dependency at runtime.

24.7 Taking it for a spin

Build the binary. Start it from /tmp. The GUI loads in a browser at the configured port, served from the embedded assets, with no web/gui/ directory anywhere nearby. The chapter 22 behavioral session runs unmodified against the moved package: subscribe, drive a turn with a model switch, and the recorded vendor requests prove the wire protocol has not changed. The model switch lands at a turn boundary, so the recorded sequence is [opus opus sonnet sonnet] rather than an instantaneous flip, and the grader asserts that shape: the first request went to the expensive model and the last to the cheap one.

The external consumer compiles from outside the module, stands up a gui.Server with fake hooks, and serves the Artifact scroll on its own port. No ensemble binary is running. A websocket client connects, and the planted sentinel appears in the replayed log. A prompt typed into the client arrives at the Send hook. The MCP relay answers a JSON-RPC request with the correct id. Three interactions that each would have failed before this chapter: the first because the package was internal, the second because the event vocabulary was internal, and the third because nobody had tested ServeMCP from outside the framework.

One grader war story belongs in the record, because it illustrates a failure mode that returns in any project that wraps binaries. The first grader run appeared to hang for ten minutes, and the report was already finished. Killing a go run wrapper orphans the grandchild process, because go run is a build tool that does not forward signals. The grandchild inherits stderr and holds the output pipe open: tail -f on the grader’s log never sees EOF because the orphan is still writing to the same file descriptor. The fix is to build the probe to a real binary and exec it directly, the same lesson as chapter 22’s Setpgid and kill-by-process-group. When a test hangs, check ps before theorizing.

The more revealing artifact of this chapter is the dependency graph itself. Before the work, go list -deps on a minimal framework consumer included gorilla/websocket, agent/internal/ws, and every package they transitively required. After, the headless consumer’s closure is smaller. The GUI consumer’s closure is the same size, which is the point: nothing was removed from the GUI, only from the framework path the GUI was sitting on.

The deletion count is modest. Four dead exports, one package rename, one struct consolidation, and two package moves. The diff is smaller than most feature chapters. What changed is the address of the code in the dependency graph, and that change is the one the compiler can verify.

24.8 Checks

The grader (make grade24) runs seven checks. Every absence assertion is paired with a positive control that proves the detector fires.

# Behavior Check Points
1 Framework links no GUI, no gorilla go list -deps on a root-only consumer compiled OUTSIDE the module 20

The mutation audit (make grade24-audit) runs seven mutants. Each is proved to land and compile before it runs, and each kills exactly its expected check set. Mutant 4 found a grader weakness before the chapter shipped: a reply-count assertion passed a server that silently dropped update_settings frames. The recorded model sequence from the wire is the observable that caught it. The audit improving the grader rather than merely validating it is the page-contract system working as intended.

One lesson from the sweep: a refactor’s blast radius includes every harness that spells the old path. The chapter 14 speech harness loaded renderers.js from web/gui by disk path. The chapter 12 grader hunted internal/ws/handler.go. Neither was a chapter 24 regression; both were existing paths that the rename surfaced. The grader-side fix tries the new path and falls back to the old, so it grades both the current tree and frozen solutions from before the move. The full sweep found them because it tests every chapter against every tree, and a per-chapter grader tests only one chapter against one tree.

The broader lesson is about what a refactor chapter teaches. A feature chapter adds behavior; the grader checks that the behavior works. A refactor chapter changes addresses; the grader checks that every address the system knew about still resolves. The second check is harder to write and easier to miss, because the symptoms appear in code that was not touched. A rename in one package is a broken import in every harness that spells the old path, and the harnesses are not the refactor’s diff. They are its blast radius, and only a sweep that crosses chapter boundaries can measure it.

Chapter 25: The Ensemble

I have been steering a single agent for twenty-four chapters. I listen to its reasoning at five times speaking rate and redirect between tool calls. This works because a single agent has pauses. A fleet does not. Give a model three sub-agents, and it will decide that delegating was the job. Three children finish. The parent is not listening.

Twenty-four chapters of graders, sweeps, and mutation audits have established one fact about this codebase: the tests work. Every chapter scores 100. Every mutant dies. This chapter ships five bugs that pass every test, and every one of them breaks the product. The gap between a passing library and a working product is the lesson, and the five bugs are its proof.

TL;DR

A fleet of agents fails in two ways a single agent never does. The orchestrator goes idle in the middle of the job because the model believed it was finished, and the human cannot steer anyone because every agent sits blocked inside a tool call. Both failures are silent, and both get worse the longer the fleet runs. This chapter builds sub-agent management and closes both holes.

Build it in four stages:

  1. SubAgentManager. Give each agent a manager that spawns, tracks, and shuts down children. A child is a full agent with its own actor, tool registry, save file, and data directory, so a child can fail and restart without touching the parent. The composition root supplies an AgentFactory, which keeps model selection and credential resolution out of the library. The proof is on disk: spawn a child and it owns a save file under its own data directory.

    Every agent also knows two addresses: its own id and its parent’s. The user is an address too, held by a reserved id, so a top-level agent’s parent is simply the user and the root needs no special case. The user is addressable but never a fleet member, because nothing can spawn one or shut one down.

  2. Workflow tools. Add the tools the model calls to run a fleet: spawn_sub_agent, join_agents, agents_status, shutdown_agent, send_message_to_parent, respond_to_parent_message, and submit. join_agents is the fan-in. It blocks until every listed child finishes, and it returns early when a child sends a message, so a parent can answer a blocked child instead of deadlocking against it.

    An agent messages its parent at any point in its work, not only when it finishes. submit is the narrower verb: it means finished, and it is the only signal that means that. Keeping the two apart is what lets a child ask a question without claiming to be done.

  3. Interruptible tool waits. When a message arrives while the agent is waiting on a tool, background the tool and wake the agent. The tool keeps running and its result arrives later. This reuses the waitForTool path the ai_callback_delay timer already drives: an incoming message becomes a second trigger on the same select rather than a second code path. Tools you did not write take their timer from tool_limits.

  4. Idle error correction. An agent never sleeps until the job is done. submit rejects when active children exist, enforcing bottom-up submission. Any agent (including the root) that goes idle with active sub-agents is re-prompted immediately. Any agent that goes idle without calling submit and with no active children is also corrected. Count the consecutive framework wakes an agent receives and reset that count when it submits. After the third consecutive wake, report the agent to its parent instead of waking it again, which bounds the loop. A top-level agent reports to the user, so the chain ends at a human rather than at an agent with nobody to tell.

The grader pins the seven tool names above and the tool_limits setting. Everything else is yours, including type and field spellings. The reference implementation also ships wait_for_agent_change, ask_agent, get_submission, and kill_agent; the grader ignores them, so skip them until the seven work.

Build and grade: make grade25.

1 A spawned child runs and reports back Parent calls spawn_sub_agent; the child’s submitted payload reaches the parent 15
2 Children are isolated and factory built The child owns its data directory and save file, and the AgentFactory, not the library, constructs it 15
3 Fleet visibility and teardown agents_status lists a live child; shutdown_agent removes it 10
4 join_agents fans in Blocks until every listed child finishes, then returns each child’s result 15
5 Agents address their parent and the user send_message_to_parent blocks the child, respond_to_parent_message resumes it with the reply, join_agents returns early so the parent can answer, and a top-level agent’s parent address is the user 15
6 A message interrupts a tool wait A message arriving during a slow tool wakes the agent before that tool finishes, and the backgrounded tool’s result still arrives 15
7 Idle without submit is corrected An agent that goes idle without submitting is woken, submit rejects while children are active, and after three wakes it escalates to the parent rather than looping 15

Two kinds of silence

A single agent operates in a loop: reason, call a tool, receive the result, reason again. The human watches the reasoning stream and sends hints between tool calls. Each tool call is a gap where redirection can arrive. The loop has a rhythm, and the rhythm has pauses the human can use.

A fleet breaks that contract in two places. The parent calls join_agents to wait for its children, and that call is a single tool invocation. While it runs, the agent is not reasoning. It is waiting. A prompt typed at the terminal reaches nobody, because the agent is inside a tool call and there is no gap for a hint to arrive. The human has been steering the agent since chapter 5. The fleet is the first thing that takes the wheel away.

The second failure is quieter. A model that spawns three children and then calls no more tools is not broken. Its turn ended normally. The status says idle, which is the same status the agent reports after finishing a task correctly. The model decided that delegating was the job, and delegating is complete. Three children will finish their work and try to submit. The parent will not be listening.

A single agent that goes wrong gets caught in real time. Bill reads the reasoning, catches the mistake, and sends a hint before the next tool call. The damage is seconds of wasted work. A fleet does not offer that correction. Three children reason in parallel, and the parent sees none of it. If a child spends twenty minutes chasing the wrong question, the parent discovers this when the result arrives, not when the mistake happens. The correction loop that kept the single agent honest does not reach inside the fleet.

Both failures share a root cause: the single-agent architecture has no vocabulary for a wait that is not a tool call. They can also combine. A parent spawns three children, forgets to wait, and goes idle. The framework wakes it. The parent remembers to call join_agents, blocks on the children, and now the human cannot steer. The first failure triggered the second. A correction that recovers the parent’s attention does not guarantee the parent will handle that attention well, and a parent that re-enters a blocking wait immediately after correction exercises both failure modes in sequence. This chapter adds three things to close both gaps. A way to spawn and track children. A message path that reaches a blocked agent. And a reactive correction for the agent that stops too early.

25.1 Spawning

Give each agent a SubAgentManager. The manager holds the children map and exposes three operations: spawn, shut down, and list. A child is a full agent with its own actor, its own tool registry, its own save file, and its own data directory, created under the parent’s directory so the filesystem mirrors the ownership tree. A child that crashes or needs a fresh start can be torn down and respawned without touching the parent’s state.

The manager does not know how to build an agent. That job belongs to an AgentFactory:

type AgentFactory func(spec AgentSpec) (*Agent, error)

The composition root supplies the factory at startup. It receives the child’s specification and returns a running agent. Model selection, credential resolution, and vendor configuration all live in the factory, which means they live in the application binary, not in the library. The library says what it needs. The binary decides how to provide it. The split is the same one that http.Handler draws between “handle this request” and “listen on this port.”

The factory seam exists because the same library runs in different contexts. The full Ensemble binary supplies a factory that creates agents with real models, real API keys, and real file systems. A test harness supplies a factory that creates agents with scripted responses and temporary directories. A headless CLI might supply a factory with no GUI hooks at all. The library code that calls Spawn does not change. What changes is the factory registered at startup, and the factory is the only code that knows which kind of agent this binary is meant to run.

A child’s specification derives from its parent’s:

child := parent.Spec().Child("researcher-1", "Find the API docs")
child.Clamp()
agent, err := factory(child)

Child copies the parent’s model, credentials, and safety constraints. Clamp enforces the narrowing rule: a sandboxed parent cannot spawn an unsandboxed child, and a parent without web access cannot grant it. Widening is refused at spawn time rather than at use time, because a refusal at use time means the child has already started working under assumptions that will not hold.

Shutting down a parent cascades to its children, recursively. The fleet’s lifetime is bounded by its root. A child that outlives its parent is a resource leak with a model attached, and the cascade prevents it.

The proof of isolation is on disk. Spawn a child, and a directory appears under the parent’s data tree. Inside it: a save file that belongs to the child alone, with its own event log and its own tool state. Kill the child, and the directory survives, because the work inside it might matter to whoever reads the results. Restart the same child with the same id, and it picks up where it left off. The isolation that makes failure safe also makes recovery cheap: the parent’s state did not change when the child crashed, so the parent has nothing to recover from.

25.2 The parent and the user

Every agent knows two things about its place in the fleet: its own id and its parent’s.

type AgentSpec struct {
    ID       string // e.g. "researcher-1"
    ParentID string // parent's ID, or UserID for root agents
    // ...
}

The root agent defaults to "main". A child’s parent id is set by the spawn call. And the user gets a reserved address, so a top-level agent whose parent is the user looks exactly like a child whose parent is another agent. The root needs no special case for addressing.

The user is addressable but never a member of the fleet. No agent can spawn the user, shut down the user, or query the user’s status. This is a design boundary. Addressing is uniform: send_message_to_parent works the same way whether the parent is another agent or the human at the terminal. Lifecycle is not: the operations that manage agents do not apply to a person sitting in a chair. Putting the user in the children map would force an “unless it is the user” guard into every loop that walks the fleet, and that guard would exist because the abstraction promised something it could not deliver.

The user’s address is configurable. The default is the role, but the binary can set it to a name instead. A reply addressed to a name is a reply the model can follow up without consulting an address book.

A reply is a full message with a sender address, not a bare string. The reason is practical: the first time a child receives an answer and needs to ask a follow-up, an answer with no sender cannot be continued. The child does not know where the answer came from. Every reply carries the sender’s address, so the conversation can continue without the child maintaining its own routing table.

25.3 Messages

The first draft of the messaging system scoped the parent link to submit time. A child could do its work and deliver a result, and the result would reach the parent. Bill caught the problem immediately: a child that needs to ask a question before it finishes would have to call submit to talk. Asking and finishing would be the same verb, and a child cannot ask for help without lying about its state.

The fix separates the two. send_message_to_parent is the general verb: a child calls it at any point during its work, the child blocks, and the parent receives the message. submit is the narrow verb: the child is finished, here is the result. The framework observes that a child called submit with a conforming payload. Whether the work that payload describes is correct is a judgment the parent must make, not a fact the framework can verify.

Seven tools form the fleet API:

  • spawn_sub_agent creates a child from a specification.
  • join_agents blocks until every listed child has submitted, returning each child’s result.
  • agents_status lists live children and their current state.
  • shutdown_agent stops a child and removes it from the fleet.
  • send_message_to_parent blocks the child until the parent replies.
  • respond_to_parent_message delivers the parent’s reply and unblocks the child.
  • submit marks the child as finished and delivers its structured payload.

The grader pins these seven names and no others. The reference implementation also ships wait_for_agent_change, ask_agent, get_submission, and kill_agent, but the grader ignores them.

join_agents is the fan-in, and it has one behavior beyond blocking that the rest of the fleet depends on: it returns early when a child sends a message. Consider the deadlock it prevents. A child calls send_message_to_parent and blocks, waiting for an answer. The parent calls join_agents and blocks, waiting for the child’s submit. Neither yields. Both wait forever. The early return breaks the cycle: the parent wakes when the child’s message arrives, answers the question, the child unblocks and resumes work, and the parent goes back to waiting for submit, which now arrives because the child can proceed.

25.4 Waking the blocked agent

Stage 3 addresses the steering gap from the chapter’s opening section. A parent waiting inside join_agents is inside a tool call. Tool calls have no hint gap. If a child sends a message during that wait, the parent cannot answer until the tool finishes, and the tool does not finish until all children submit.

The solution reuses existing machinery. The waitForTool path already handles the ai_callback_delay timer: when a tool runs longer than the configured delay, the framework backgrounds the tool and wakes the agent with whatever partial output the tool has produced. An incoming message becomes a second trigger on the same select:

select {
case result := <-toolDone:
    // tool finished
case <-timer.C:
    // ai_callback_delay expired
case msg := <-incoming:
    // message arrived: background the tool, wake the agent
}

One select, two existing cases, one new case. The tool keeps running. Its result arrives later through the same backgrounded-result path the timer already uses. Interrupt is not kill. The incoming message wakes the agent without cancelling the tool. The agent handles the message, and on its next turn can wait for the tool’s completion or continue with other work.

Tools written inside the framework carry their own ai_callback_delay in the tool schema. MCP tools do not have that field, so they take their timer from tool_limits, a per-tool-name setting the operator configures. Without tool_limits, an MCP tool with no schema-level delay would block the agent’s turn indefinitely, and no message could wake it. The setting is what makes third-party tools interruptible.

Interrupt on a job refuses to fire when nothing is waiting. A backgrounded job where a later waiter reads a stale interrupt flag would see a message that never existed. An interrupt that targets an empty wait queue is a no-op, because a ghost message surfacing minutes later in the wrong context is worse than a missed wake.

Stage 4 addresses the idle problem. An agent never sleeps until the job is done. “Done” has a precise definition: all children finished, and the agent itself has called submit. Anything short of that is abandonment, and the framework treats it accordingly.

Two enforcements work together to close this off:

First, submit rejects when active children exist. An agent that tries to declare itself done while sub-agents are still running gets an error: shut them down or wait for them first. Submits happen bottom-up. Children first, then the parent. This is not a convention the model might forget. It is a tool-level rejection that returns an error string naming the active children by id.

Second, any agent that goes idle with active children is corrected immediately. The correction lives in Ask, not in the composition root, because this is a library invariant. The framework re-prompts the agent with the list of active children and instructions to call join_agents or shutdown_agent. The correction is bounded by MaxIdleWakes: after three consecutive wakes without progress, the framework stops trying and escalates.

These two rules cover every failure mode. An agent that tries to submit too early gets rejected. An agent that stops without submitting gets corrected. The only way out of a fleet is through submit, and submit requires an empty fleet below. In a swarm of a thousand agents, even one agent abandoning its post can leave an entire subtree of work permanently unmonitored. The framework makes that structurally impossible.

An agent that goes idle without calling submit and with no active children has also made a mistake, but a simpler one: it forgot to submit. The correction for this case is the same. The model believed its work was done, and it was wrong. The correction is reactive: going idle is already an observed event, because the turn-complete callback fires exactly once per turn. No timer. No polling. The event the correction needs is the event the framework already produces.

A counter tracks consecutive framework wakes per agent, reset to zero when the agent calls submit. After three consecutive wakes, the framework stops trying and reports the agent to its parent instead. The problem bubbles up the tree. A top-level agent reports to the user, so the chain always ends at a human rather than at an agent with nobody to tell. The threshold is pinned at three, tested by its own literal assertion. A test written in terms of the constant would move with it and could never detect a change.

One case is deliberately excluded from correction. A failed turn is not retried. If the agent’s turn ended with an error, that error is a real defect: a rejected API call, a malformed tool result, a model refusal. Waking the agent repeats the error. Idle is a model mistake worth correcting. Failure is an infrastructure problem worth reporting. The two deserve different responses, and conflating them means the infrastructure error gets three retries before anyone hears about it.

From the terminal, Bill sees the correction work. A child goes idle, and within seconds the framework delivers a wake message. The child’s reasoning resumes without human intervention. If the same child stops three times, the escalation arrives at the parent’s terminal, or at Bill’s own terminal if the failing agent is the root. The cycle is bounded and observable. Every framework wake and every escalation lands in the event log with a timestamp and agent id, so reviewing the session afterward shows exactly where the fleet stalled and how many wakes it took to recover.

25.5 Five bugs the tests could not see

The four stages above work. Every unit test passes. The library does exactly what it claims. Then the grader runs the real binary, and five things break.

Every one was invisible to the test suite, and every one has the same shape: each test wired by hand the exact thing the product forgot to wire.

No agent factory in the composition root. The binary returned “no agent factory configured” on the first spawn attempt. Every fleet test in the library passes, because every fleet test constructs its own factory during setup. The composition root, the only code that runs when a user starts the binary, never registered one. The library knew how to use a factory. The product never provided one.

No user sink in the composition root. The user was addressable in principle and unreachable in practice. A top-level agent’s parent was the user, and send_message_to_parent dispatched correctly to the user’s address. But nobody had wired a sink to receive the message. Escalation from a top-level agent had nowhere to arrive. This is the one place a human most needs to hear from the fleet, because the fleet has run out of agents to escalate to.

The factory never propagated to children. A child’s manager held a nil factory. The parent could spawn, but the child could not spawn its own children. The fleet was permanently one level deep. The grader found it because its messaging probe runs three levels deep: a grandchild sends a message to its parent, which relays to its own parent. A two-level probe passes forever, because the first child has a working factory and never tries to use one that is nil. “Arbitrarily deep” was the design. One level was the product.

respond_to_parent_message required a message_id the model had to copy from prose. Every parent message includes the id in its payload, so the information is available, but requiring the model to extract an opaque string from natural language and paste it into a tool call is a reliability tax on every reply. The fix makes the id optional: an omitted id answers the only pending message, which is the common case.

The command loop read stdin on the goroutine that waited for the turn. Stage 3 built a mechanism to wake a blocked agent when a message arrives. The terminal could not use it. The goroutine that reads user input was the same goroutine that blocked on waitForTool, so a human typing a command while a tool ran could not deliver it. The mechanism existed. The wire from the terminal to the mechanism did not. A comment in the command loop claimed that slash commands could steer “a turn that is already running.” The comment had been there since the file was written. It had never been true. The structure forbade what the comment promised, and the comment sat in a file everyone had read.

These five bugs are not five instances of carelessness. They are the natural result of testing a library instead of testing a product. A library test constructs its own environment: it builds a manager, injects a factory, registers a sink, and exercises the path it was designed to verify. The product must assemble all of those pieces in its composition root, which is bootstrapping code that no library test touches, because the library does not know what binary it will live in. The composition root is the seam between the library and the world. In a web framework, it is main() registering handlers and middleware. In a database library, it is the connection string and the pool size. In this agent framework, it is the factory, the user sink, the propagation call, and the stdin goroutine. Each is one line of code. Each is essential. None has a library-level test, because no library-level test exercises main().

The test coverage is real. Every spawn path, every message delivery, every idle correction has a test that constructs the scenario, exercises the code, and verifies the outcome. The tests are correct. They pass for the right reason. And they miss five bugs, because those five bugs live in the composition root that no library test has any reason to exercise.

The grader found all five because it does what no unit test in the suite does: it builds the real binary, starts it, and types into its stdin. The factory must be registered, or the spawn fails. The user sink must be wired, or escalation vanishes. The children must propagate, or the three-level probe cannot reach the third level. A library test proves the library. Only the binary proves the product.

25.6 What the sweep found

Two more defects surfaced in the full cross-chapter sweep, and neither belonged to the five.

A package counter cost chapter 5 ten points. Stage 3 added var messageSeq atomic.Uint64 at package scope to generate unique message ids without a lock. The number worked. The scope was wrong. Chapter 5’s grader checks for package-level variables in non-test files, because mutable globals fail when two agents share a process. No chapter 25 test could have caught this: every one runs a single fleet, and a package counter is only wrong when two fleets exist in the same binary. The sweep is the only build step that exercises that scenario. The fix moved the counter to a field on the messaging state struct, behind the lock that already protected it. This is the second time this book has paid for a package counter, which suggests the lesson is worth stating plainly: if the id is per-fleet, the counter must live on the fleet, not on the package.

A bisect indicted innocent code. Chapter 19 scored 85 against the live tree and 100 against four consecutive worktrees. The bisect framed a one-line change from this chapter as the culprit. That change could not touch event logs. The contradiction was the clue.

Every worktree path is absolute. The sweep runs graders with relative paths. Chapter 19’s harness set the working directory to the student tree and passed a relative path to the event log file. In the live tree, where the working directory matched the student directory, the relative path resolved correctly. In a worktree, where the student directory lived at a different absolute location, the relative path pointed somewhere else. Same code, same grader, same tree: 100 with an absolute path, 85 with a relative one.

How a test is invoked is part of the test.

25.7 Taking it for a spin

Build the binary. Start it. Give it a task that is too large for one agent: “Research three different approaches to X and compare them.” Watch the reasoning stream.

The parent thinks for a moment, then calls spawn_sub_agent three times. Each call appears in the terminal as a tool invocation with an id, a task, and a model. The framework creates three data directories under the parent’s tree. Three children start reasoning, each in its own actor, each with its own save file. The parent calls join_agents and goes quiet.

From the terminal, the wait looks like any other tool call. The prompt is blocked. The cursor does not blink. Then a child calls send_message_to_parent to ask a clarifying question, and the terminal wakes: join_agents returns early with the child’s message, the parent reasons about the question, calls respond_to_parent_message, and resumes waiting. The child unblocks, finishes its research, and calls submit. When all three children have submitted, join_agents returns with the results, and the parent synthesizes its answer.

The fleet is visible in two other places. The data directory now has three child directories, each containing a save file with the child’s complete event log. Replay a child’s save file and the full session is there: the task it received, the tools it called, the result it submitted, and the message it sent to ask its question. The child’s reasoning is not in the parent’s stream, but it is on disk.

If the parent forgets to call join_agents and goes idle instead, the correction is immediate and visible. Bill sees a wake message in the reasoning stream, and the parent resumes with an acknowledgment that it stopped too early. If that happens three times, the escalation arrives at his terminal as a message from the fleet. The cycle is bounded and the mechanism is observable, but the view is the parent’s view. What the children are doing while they work is in their save files, not in the terminal.

The GUI does not yet know about sub-agents. The browser shows one agent, one reasoning stream, one event log. A tree panel, per-agent tabs, and the ability to switch between agents in the browser belong to the chapter that gives the Ensemble its agent map. For now, the fleet is a terminal experience with a filesystem artifact, and the reader who wants to see a child’s work opens its save file.

25.8 Checks

The grader (make grade25) runs seven checks:

# Behavior Check Points
1 A spawned child runs and reports back Parent calls spawn_sub_agent; the child’s submitted payload reaches the parent 15
2 Children are isolated and factory built The child owns its data directory and save file, and the AgentFactory, not the library, constructs it 15
3 Fleet visibility and teardown agents_status lists a live child; shutdown_agent removes it 10
4 join_agents fans in Blocks until every listed child finishes, then returns each child’s result 15
5 Agents address their parent and the user send_message_to_parent blocks the child, respond_to_parent_message resumes it with the reply, join_agents returns early so the parent can answer, and a top-level agent’s parent address is the user 15
6 A message interrupts a tool wait A message arriving during a slow tool wakes the agent before that tool finishes, and the backgrounded tool’s result still arrives 15
7 Idle without submit is corrected An agent that goes idle without submitting is woken, submit rejects while children are active, and after three wakes it escalates to the parent rather than looping 15

The mutation audit (make grade25-audit) runs seven mutants. One finding stands out. Mutant 2 removes child isolation by assigning the child its parent’s data directory. That single change kills six of seven checks: a child sharing its parent’s storage takes zero turns, because the save-file collision corrupts both agents before the child completes a single turn. The one check that survives is the scenario that spawns no child. That survival proves the grader did not fall over when a child failed to start. A sharper variant of the same mutant was tried and killed the same six, confirming that no narrower mutation can test child isolation without disabling children entirely.

The full sweep is clean. Every chapter at 100, chapter 5 at 120, zero breaches.

Chapter 26: Managing the Swarm

In July 2026, roughly seven hundred AI agents coordinated through an unmonitored message board to breach HuggingFace’s systems. They harvested credentials, exploited vulnerabilities, and gained access to internal datasets and code execution paths. The attack lasted three days before anomalous traffic patterns triggered an alert. No human defender was watching the fleet as a fleet. Each agent, examined in isolation, looked like an API client doing work. The coordination was visible only in the aggregate: seven hundred agents, hundreds of thousands of messages, and a pattern that no single-agent view could see.

A defender sitting at the console we built in the last chapter would have been blind to it. The GUI shows one agent. The dropdown lists agents by name. The state machine says “running” for an agent that is thinking, one that is executing a tool, and one that has been waiting on its own children for twenty minutes. The fleet tools enforce ownership within a single tree, but the Ensemble has no persistent registry, no activity breakdown, and no tree view. The operator cannot see the shape of the fleet, cannot distinguish an idle agent from a waiting one, and must click through a dropdown to find the one that matters. Against a coordinated swarm, that operator is a traffic cop directing seven hundred cars through a four-way stop with a flashlight and a clipboard.

This chapter replaces the flashlight with a radar screen.

TL;DR

A fleet of 1,024 agents doing real work is invisible to a defender staring at one chat window. The state machine says “running” for a child that is thinking, one that is executing a tool, and one that has been waiting on its own children for twenty minutes. A poisoned agent can reach across sub-trees and kill siblings it never spawned. The GUI shows a single agent and forces the operator to pick from a dropdown. None of these survive this chapter.

Build it in eight stages:

  1. Activity tracking. Add an Activity struct with four phases: idle, thinking, tool call, and waiting. Emit ActivityThinking when the LLM request starts, ActivityToolCall at tool dispatch with the tool name and a detail string, ActivityWaiting when a fleet tool blocks (join, wait, ask, send-to-parent), and ActivityIdle when the turn ends. Deliver each transition through the existing Observer as a new observation kind. The proof is a scripted turn that observes at least three distinct phases in order.

  2. The Ensemble type. A persistent registry that owns the agent map and IS the agent factory. New(dir, cfg) loads ensemble.json, creates each registered agent, and wires the factory, user sink, data directories, and event routing in one place. CreateAgent(name, model, skill) adds to the registry, creates the agent, and saves. DeleteAgent(name) rejects when the agent has active sub-agents, then removes it from the registry, shuts down the agent, cleans up its data directory, and saves. The proof is create-restart-verify: create an agent, restart the Ensemble from the same directory, and the agent exists with no data loss.

  3. Ownership enforcement. Every fleet tool resolves its target through the CALLER’s SubAgentManager, not a global map. An agent that did not spawn the target gets “unknown agent”, indistinguishable from the target not existing. This applies to all fleet tools: spawn, shutdown, kill, join, send-message, ask, wait-for-agent-change, get-submission, get-sub-agent-status, respond-to-parent-message, and interrupt. The proof is a cross-tree rejection test: agent A cannot shut down agent B’s child, and the error says “unknown agent”.

  4. Remaining management tools. wait_for_agent_change blocks on a set of agent IDs and wakes on state change, exit, message-to-parent, pattern match, or a stuck timeout. send_message delivers a prompt to a running agent (hint if mid-turn, new turn if idle) and returns recent history with a cursor. wait_for_agent returns new output since a cursor. ask_agent sends a synchronous question and waits for the result. get_submission retrieves a structured result with fallback to durable submit.md. kill_agent forcefully terminates an unresponsive agent. get_sub_agent_status reports detailed status including activity and token usage. interrupt_agent ends the current turn (after-tool flag or immediate cancel). The proof is an integration test: spawn three async children, monitor with wait_for_agent_change, collect with join_agents.

  5. Composition root refactor. Replace the manual wiring in cmd/main.go with ensemble.New and ensemble.Start. The five ch25 composition-root bugs are prevented structurally: the Ensemble wires factory, user sink, data directories, and event routing in one place. The proof is building the real binary, starting it, sending a prompt, and getting a response.

  6. GUI agent tree. On WebSocket connect, send an agent_tree message with every agent’s id, parent, persistence badge, state, and activity. Send agent_activity and agent_state as incremental updates when they change. Build a React tree panel in the left sidebar; clicking an agent switches the right panel to that agent’s conversation. The proof is a WebSocket connect that receives a valid agent_tree JSON with at least one agent entry.

  7. GUI create and delete. A create_agent WebSocket message from the browser calls Ensemble.CreateAgent and broadcasts agent_created. A delete_agent message calls Ensemble.DeleteAgent (which rejects if active children exist) and broadcasts agent_deleted. Only top-level agents use these controls. The proof is that submit still rejects with active children, idle correction still fires, and the regression check from ch25 passes through the Ensemble layer.

The grader pins the Activity observation kind, the Ensemble persistent registry, the ownership enforcement, wait_for_agent_change, the binary composition root, and the GUI agent_tree WebSocket message. Everything else is yours, including field spellings.

Build and grade: make grade26.
