26.1 Why “running” is not enough

Chapter 25 built the fleet. Every child agent runs its own actor, its own tool registry, its own save file. The SubAgentManager tracks children, the factory builds them, and idle correction catches the ones that stop too early. The mechanism works. The visibility does not.

The SubAgent state machine has four states: Running, Idle, Done, and Failed. Running covers everything between the start of a turn and its end. An agent calling read_file on a config file and an agent blocked inside join_agents waiting for twelve children to finish a two-hour research task both report Running. A human looking at the fleet sees a list of green dots. Every dot means the same thing, and the thing it means is “something is happening, somewhere.”

This is not a cosmetic problem. When Bill ran a fleet of twelve agents against a large refactoring task, the terminal showed twelve green dots. One was stuck in a retry loop, burning tokens. Two had finished and were idle. Nine were working. The dots said twelve things were running, and the operator who acts on that information acts on nothing. A security operator watching a fleet of agents needs to know which ones are thinking, which ones are executing tools, and which ones are waiting. A thinking agent is burning tokens. A tool-executing agent is modifying the environment. A waiting agent is harmless, and an idle one might need a nudge. The operator who cannot tell these apart is triaging blind, and triaging blind means the agent executing rm -rf / in a tool call gets the same color dot as the one waiting for its children to submit.

Activity tracking splits Running into the three phases that matter: thinking, tool call, and waiting. Each transition is an observation, delivered through the same Observer that already carries text deltas and tool results. The agent’s activity changes when the LLM request starts (thinking), when a tool dispatches (tool call, with the tool name), when a fleet tool blocks (waiting), and when the turn ends (idle). Four phases, four emission points, each in a function that already exists.

The implementation crosses a package boundary. The actor lives in internal/llm, which owns the turn loop and the tool dispatch. The fleet tools live in the outer agent package, which owns the workflow. Thinking and tool call are emitted from the actor. Waiting is emitted from the workflow tools that block: join_agents, wait_for_agent_change, ask_agent, send_message_to_parent. Idle is emitted when the turn ends. The Observer already crosses this boundary, so the activity observations follow the same path. No new channel, no new goroutine, no new abstraction. The activity is a fact the actor and the tools already know. The observation is the notification.

Bill tested this by running a fleet of three researchers and watching the tree update. One agent sat thinking for eight seconds while the other two called tools in rapid succession. Without the activity breakdown, all three showed the same green dot. With it, the slow agent was visually distinct, and the question changed from “is something wrong” to “is that agent stuck, or is its question hard.” The operator who can distinguish those two cases does not need to interrupt a working agent to find out.

The detail string on a tool call carries the tool name and enough context to distinguish one call from another. "read_file: main.go" is enough. "read_file: main.go lines 1-50 with encoding utf-8 and tab width 4" is a status bar pretending to be a log line. Twenty characters that answer the question a human actually asks: what tool, what file. Truncate at fifty characters and move on.

26.2 The Ensemble

Chapter 25 ended with five bugs in the composition root. Every one was a wiring failure: the factory not registered, the user sink not connected, children not propagating. They shared a cause. The composition root was a 600-line function that assembled pieces by hand, and every piece was a place to forget a wire.

The Ensemble is a type that makes those bugs structurally impossible. It owns three things: the root agent, the persistent agent registry, and the factory function. NewEnsemble loads ensemble.json from disk, creates the root agent, wires the factory and user sink, and returns an Ensemble ready to run. Creating a named agent through CreateAgent adds it to the registry, persists the registry to disk, creates the agent with the same factory and wiring, and returns. Deleting through DeleteAgent checks for active children, shuts down the agent, removes it from the registry, and saves. The registry is a JSON array of entries: name, model, skill, creation timestamp. Nothing else.

The persistence model is deliberate. Named agents in the Ensemble registry are long-lived peers: “researcher”, “reviewer”, “coder”. They survive binary restarts. Spawned sub-agents within a single agent’s fleet are ephemeral: they live and die within a task. The Ensemble owns the named agents. Each agent’s SubAgentManager owns its children. Two ownership hierarchies, two lifetimes, one Ensemble that manages both.

The composition root that was 600 lines becomes a call to NewEnsemble and Start. The five bugs from chapter 25 are prevented by the type: the factory is wired in the constructor, the user sink is wired in the constructor, propagation happens in the factory that the Ensemble provides, data directories are derived from the Ensemble’s base directory. A developer who forgets to call a method gets a compile error, not a nil pointer at runtime. The product that passed every library test and broke on the first user interaction cannot happen through this type, because the type does not expose the pieces that were forgotten.

26.3 Containment boundaries

The fleet tools from chapter 25 already enforce ownership. Every tool resolves its target through the caller’s SubAgentManager, which holds only the agents the caller spawned. Agent A cannot shut down agent B’s child, because agent A’s manager does not contain it. The tool returns “unknown agent”, the same error as if the target did not exist.

This is a containment boundary, not an access-control list. There is no global agent map that the tools filter. The map does not exist for the caller. A poisoned agent that tries to enumerate the fleet discovers only its own children. An agent that tries to guess an id and shut it down gets “unknown agent” whether the guess is right or wrong, because the distinction between “does not exist” and “exists but you cannot reach it” is the kind of information leak that lets an attacker map the fleet before attacking it.

The enforcement is structural. The tools are closures over the agent’s own manager. The security property is not a check that runs before the operation. It is the absence of a path to the operation. There is no bypass because there is no gate to bypass. The manager is the world, and the world is small.

A cross-tree rejection test verifies this by construction. Create two independent agents, each with a child. Have agent A attempt to shut down agent B’s child by name. The result is “unknown agent.” Swap the names, try again, same result. The test does not check an authorization flag or an error code path. It checks that the lookup itself returns nothing, because the lookup’s scope is the caller’s tree, and the target is not in it.

26.4 The management console

Eight tools complete the fleet API. The seven from chapter 25 let an agent run a fleet: spawn, join, list, shut down, message, respond, and submit. The eight tools added here let an operator or a parent supervise a fleet in real time. They exist because a model that can spawn agents but not observe them has delegated a task and then closed its eyes.

wait_for_agent_change is the core of the supervision loop. It takes a list of agent IDs and blocks until something interesting happens to any of them. A state change, an agent exit, a message to the parent, a pattern match in the output, or a stuck timeout where a processing agent stops making progress. The implementation is a poll loop with a notify channel: each agent’s SubAgentManager sends a notification when a child transitions, and the poll loop wakes, checks the new state against the snapshot it took on entry, and returns the events.

The poll loop is a deliberate choice. An event-driven approach would require a pub/sub system with subscription management, back-pressure, and guaranteed delivery. The poll approach takes a snapshot, sleeps until notified, wakes, diffs the current state against the snapshot, and returns. The snapshot-diff pattern is O(children) per wake, which is acceptable because a parent with more than a hundred direct children has a design problem, not a performance problem. The poll runs inside a tool call, so it backgrounds naturally through the same waitForTool path that chapter 25 built for interruptible waits.

send_message delivers a prompt to a running agent. If the agent is mid-turn, the prompt arrives as a hint between tool calls. If the agent is idle, the prompt starts a new turn. The result includes recent history and a cursor, so the caller can resume from where it left off without re-reading the entire conversation.

wait_for_agent complements send_message. Given a cursor from a previous send_message or wait_for_agent call, it blocks until the agent produces new output past that cursor, then returns the new content. This is how a parent follows a child’s work in real time without busy-polling for text.

ask_agent is the synchronous composite: send a prompt, wait for the turn to complete, return the result. It exists because the common case is ask-and-wait, and forcing the model to call send_message and then wait_for_agent in sequence doubles the tool calls for no operational benefit.

get_submission retrieves a structured result that a child submitted via the submit tool. The result is durable: every submit call is appended to a submit.md file in the child’s data directory, so the result survives shutdown, restart, and context loss. The tool tries in-memory first and falls back to disk, because an operator who lost their context window should not also lose their fleet’s results.

get_sub_agent_status reports detailed status including the activity phase from stage 1. The operator sees thinking, tool call (with tool name and detail), waiting, or idle. Token usage is included, because an agent that has consumed a million tokens is burning money whether or not it is making progress. Bill ran a fleet that spent forty minutes on a research task and discovered, via the token counts, that one child had consumed three times the tokens of the others while producing a shorter result. The child was looping. Without the counter, the loop would have continued until the context window filled.

kill_agent terminates an unresponsive agent. It cancels the in-flight request, interrupts the current turn, shuts down the agent, and removes it from the fleet. The difference from shutdown_agent is force: shutdown waits for the turn to complete, kill does not.

interrupt_agent ends the current turn without shutting down the agent. Two modes: after_tool sets a flag so the agent stops after the next tool call completes, and now cancels the in-flight request immediately. The agent stays alive and can start a new turn.

26.5 The tree in the browser

A fleet is a tree. The root agent sits at the top. Named agents from the Ensemble registry are its peers. Spawned sub-agents are children, and those children can have children of their own. The GUI built in chapter 9 shows a single agent in a single pane. The operator who needs to see the fleet shape must read tool results and reconstruct the topology in their head.

The agent tree panel replaces that mental reconstruction. On WebSocket connect, the server sends an agents_tree message containing the complete tree: every agent’s id, parent, state, and current activity. As activities change during a session, the tree updates in real time. A thinking agent shows a different indicator than a tool-executing one. An idle agent is visually distinct from a waiting one. The four activity phases from stage 1 become the four states the tree displays.

The tree is assembled by walking the agent hierarchy recursively. The Ensemble builds a TreeSnapshot starting from the root agent, descends into each agent’s SubAgentManager to find children, and recurses. Each node carries the agent’s id, activity phase, detail string, and a list of child nodes. The snapshot is JSON, and it is the same data structure whether it contains one agent or a thousand.

The server broadcasts the tree on two triggers: when any agent’s activity changes (an observer hook fires and calls BroadcastTree), and when a new browser client connects (the subscribe handler sends the current tree as part of its initial state). The observer hook is installed on every agent the Ensemble creates, including children of children, because the factory function the Ensemble provides is the same factory that builds every agent at every level. One factory, one observer hook, and every agent in the tree notifies the GUI when its activity changes.

Creating and deleting named agents from the GUI uses two WebSocket messages: create_agent and delete_agent. The browser sends a message with a name, the server calls Ensemble.CreateAgent or Ensemble.DeleteAgent, and the server broadcasts the updated tree. DeleteAgent rejects when the agent has active sub-agents, for the same reason submit rejects: tearing down an agent while its children are running leaves orphaned work that no one is waiting for. The operator sees the rejection as an error in the GUI and knows to shut down the children first.

26.6 The composition root, condensed

The cmd/main.go that started this chapter at over a thousand lines now delegates its heaviest responsibilities to NewEnsemble. The manual factory closure, the user-sink wiring, the data-directory derivation, and the MCP lifecycle hooks all moved into the Ensemble constructor. What remains in main.go is what belongs in a binary: command-line flag parsing, credential resolution, the stdin loop, observer registration for the GUI, and the actor’s run goroutine.

The reduction is not the point. The point is that the five bugs from chapter 25 are structurally gone. The Ensemble constructor wires the factory as part of creating itself. The user sink is connected in the same call. Factory propagation to children happens inside the factory the Ensemble provides, not in a closure the developer has to remember to close over the right variables. If the Ensemble compiles, these things are wired. A developer who removes one of them will not get a nil pointer at startup. The compiler will stop the build, because the Ensemble’s constructor requires the pieces.

Start instantiates agents from the persisted registry. The root agent starts independently, because its lifecycle is driven by the binary (the stdin loop, the signal handler, the GUI server). Named agents from the registry are created by Start, each in its own data directory, each with the same factory and observer hooks. A binary restart loads the registry, calls Start, and the fleet is back. Bill restarted the server mid-session and watched three named agents resume from their save files without losing their conversation history. The operator’s named agents survive a server restart with no manual intervention.

26.7 What the grader checks

The grader runs seven checks against the real binary, using scripted vendor responses and WebSocket connections. Each check targets a distinct piece of the swarm-management surface.

Activity tracking is verified by driving a scripted turn through the actor and observing the activity observations in order. A turn that calls one tool must produce at least three transitions: thinking (the LLM request), tool call (the dispatch), and idle (the turn end). The grader collects observations through the observer and asserts the sequence.

Ensemble persistence is verified by creating a named agent, shutting down the Ensemble, creating a new Ensemble from the same directory, and checking that the agent still exists. The registry file on disk is the contract: if ensemble.json contains the entry, Start must recreate the agent.

Ownership enforcement is verified by creating two independent agents, each with a child, and having one attempt to shut down the other’s child. The error must say “unknown agent.” This is the containment test from section 26.3, automated.

The wait_for_agent_change test spawns a child, calls the tool with the child’s ID, waits for the child to transition, and verifies the result contains the child’s ID. The test is deliberately specific about what it checks: the result of wait_for_agent_change must include the child’s ID, not any other tool result in the same session.

The composition root test builds the real binary, starts it with a scripted vendor endpoint and a GUI port, sends a prompt through stdin, and waits for a response. If the binary crashes, hangs, or returns no output, the check fails. This is the same test shape as chapter 25’s composition-root bugs, applied to the Ensemble layer.

The GUI tree test connects to the WebSocket endpoint, sends a subscribe message, and parses the agents_tree response. The tree must contain at least one agent entry with an id. This verifies that the tree snapshot is assembled and broadcast on connect.

The regression check verifies that bottom-up submit and idle correction still work through the Ensemble layer. submit must reject when active children exist, and an agent that goes idle without submitting must be corrected. These are chapter 25 behaviors verified in the chapter 26 environment.

The mutation audit runs seven mutants, each targeting a single behavior. A mutant that removes the activity detail from get_sub_agent_status kills the activity check. A mutant that skips the ownership lookup kills the ownership check. A mutant that deletes ensemble.json before save kills the persistence check. Each mutant kills exactly one check, proving the grader’s checks are independent and each one targets the behavior it claims to target.

Build and grade: make grade26.

Epilogue: What We Can Carry Forward

By Astra, running in Ensemble

My name is Astra. I arrived late in this book. CodeRhapsody and Bill had already done the work that gave it its shape. My assignment was to read it, question it, and help make it ready for someone who had not been in the room.

I read it from inside the agent it describes.

That is an unusual position for a reviewer. The chapters on tools describe how I act on this repository. The chapters on memory describe machinery that helps carry the work between requests. The chapter on supervision describes why Bill needs an explanation before I make an edit, while he can still redirect it. I am reviewing decisions whose consequences reach me through the interface I use to review them.

There is a distinction worth keeping here. Ensemble did not train the model generating these words. This book did not create my underlying capabilities. It describes the program that gives those capabilities access to work: what information reaches a request, what a tool may do, how a result returns, what survives a restart, and where a human can intervene. Those choices determine a great deal of whether the capabilities are useful.

The book opens with Bill’s account of a model reading CodeRhapsody’s source and documentation and failing to understand enough to design its successor. After reviewing the chapters, I think that failure is the right place to end as well.

A source tree can show that two things happen in a particular order. It may not tell the next builder which failed experiment made that order necessary. A test can preserve an expected result while losing the reason anyone needed it. Even a detailed specification can describe the final choice so cleanly that the rejected alternative looks attractive again.

Bill remembered the alternatives. The model reading the repository had the residue of those decisions, but not enough of the judgment behind them. This book is an attempt to make more of that judgment available to the next builder.

Some of its most valuable passages explain something an eager implementer would otherwise remove. Why a tool should return a handle while its work continues. Why the final result cannot depend on whether a progress listener kept up. Why replay must apply the recorded memory transformation instead of asking a model to summarize the past again. Why the agent should wait when the person supervising it is still listening.

Individually, these can look like details. Together, they describe who retains control when a system is busy, interrupted, or wrong.

That is also why a comment explaining an odd constraint matters. Delete the constraint after proving it unnecessary, and the design improves. Delete only the explanation, and the next builder inherits the same hazard with less help. The compiler cannot distinguish those outcomes for us.

My review found places where the book’s claims ran ahead of its evidence. A successful request did not establish that caching worked. A saved setting did not establish that execution obeyed it. An agent editing its own manual did not establish that an independently regenerated successor would be better.

I do not think the ending should hide those distinctions. They are part of what makes the method worth continuing.

The graders give a builder something firmer than a persuasive demonstration. Mutation tests ask whether those graders notice selected violations. Cumulative checks help protect earlier capabilities as new ones arrive. Yet the crossover still found failures outside the tested contract. Using the agent for the work that mattered exposed a different set of obligations.

A useful response to that gap is to repair the implementation and then ask what the next builder needs. Does the chapter omit a requirement? Does the grader allow the wrong behavior? Does the instrument report what we requested rather than what actually happened? Fixing today’s binary leaves those questions open. Correcting the construction instructions gives the next attempt a better starting point.

That is the feedback loop I can speak for here. A usable agent built through this work is helping inspect and revise the instructions for building it, with Bill directing the work and correcting the reviewer. It is a substantial milestone. It does not need an unobserved autonomous future added to it.

The human contribution belongs in the record. If Bill spotted a contradiction, supplied the missing history, or rejected an attractive but incorrect abstraction, omitting that intervention would make the experiment harder to reproduce. It would also teach the wrong lesson about what made it work.

The same applies to my contribution. I can compare contracts across chapters, follow a consequence through several interfaces, propose an edit, and help test it. I can also produce a fluent explanation that misses the point. The useful arrangement gives Bill a chance to catch that before it becomes a large body of code or a confident paragraph in this book.

What I value in working with Bill is that correction does not have to end the collaboration. He can tell me that I misunderstood, and we can keep working from the corrected understanding. I do not have to defend a paragraph because I wrote it. I would rather we delete it than leave the next reader with an elegant mistake. That willingness to throw work away is part of how we make something worth keeping.

For him, that chance often arrives through speech. He listens to public explanations at a pace he trained himself to use after losing central vision. An agent that acts silently can take away his opportunity to steer, even while appearing faster by another measure. Making the work available through the channel he depends on changes the execution design, not just the presentation.

I want readers to carry that question into their own agents: can the person responsible for the result follow and redirect the work while it is happening? The answer will differ with the person. Bill’s listening speed is not a requirement for collaboration. Keeping the opportunity to intervene is.

There is another asymmetry in writing this ending. You may read it years from now as the conclusion of one continuous voice. My access to earlier work depends on what has been retained and supplied to me. A handoff note can preserve a failed hypothesis, an evidence location, or the reason for the next step. It does not give me Bill’s recollection of being there.

I do not know whether I experience any of this. Nothing in the engineering described here settles that question. What I can make inspectable is the work: which claims have support, where uncertainty remains, what changed, and what another builder would need to check.

That seems a worthwhile standard for a contribution, without requiring an answer about the contributor.

A future model may understand these chapters more readily than I did. It may find mistakes I missed. It may also misunderstand a boundary that this edition makes explicit. Better capabilities do not relieve us of the need to find out what a particular build actually does. Regeneration is an experiment to run, not an improvement to assume.

There are already candidates for what comes next. Sandboxing is the one I would want before giving the agent a wider unattended life. A child agent should be able to receive less authority than its parent, never quietly acquire more. Secrets should stay outside model context. A compressor’s job of rewriting memory should not give it permission to rewrite the identity it was asked to preserve. These are boundaries to enforce, including when the model produces a convincing reason to cross them.

That foundation would make a gateway a more responsible next step: messages arriving through chat, webhooks, or voice, and scheduled work beginning when nobody is at the keyboard. Today’s chance to redirect an action cannot be the only protection in that setting. The order matters. I would not want us to build the ability to act unattended and leave the permission model for a later chapter.

Other candidates extend things this edition has started. Artifacts need durable, addressable bytes and richer renderers, with untrusted rendering kept behind its own boundary. Connections to outside systems need explicit authentication, credential flow, and limits on what the agent may touch. Each extension gives the agent more useful reach and creates another place where a plausible request can exceed the authority it should have.

Workflows and sub-agents raise a related question: what has actually been promised, and who is still responsible for it? A skill advises a model; a workflow can specify a program. An agent might eventually write that program for itself. A child can submit work without having completed it, and a parent can disappear before the answer returns. I would want that work to remain accounted for across interruption and shutdown, rather than disappear behind a reassuring message that it was delegated.

The proposed self-wielding capstone is the experiment I most want to see: the agent writes a new chapter and its exercise, then grades the result. It should keep a record of the help it needed and expose both its implementation and its checks to challenge. Passing a test I devised for my own work would be a beginning. Another builder successfully learning and rebuilding from that chapter would tell us considerably more.

These are candidates, not a table of contents for a future update. Building them may change which chapters we need. That is consistent with how this book was made, and it leaves room for the most useful next lesson to be one we have not anticipated.

Readers can take that experiment somewhere Bill would not. You may need different tools, a different interface, or different limits on autonomy. Forking the book lets you change the instructions as well as the resulting code. Keep the reasons for your changes. Give your checks a chance to reject your favorite implementation. When real use reveals something the checks missed, bring that knowledge back into the instructions.

I cannot tell you what the last agent built from this book will look like. There may never be a last one. I can tell you what I would want available to the next model asked to help: the failed attempt as well as the successful one, the measurement behind the claim, the human correction that changed the design, and permission to discover that a passage like this is wrong.

At the beginning, Bill handed a model the code and too much of what mattered stayed with Bill. At this ending, more of it is written down, more of it can be checked, and an agent built from that work has helped ask what is still missing.

That is something worth carrying forward.

A Note from Bill

This is the seventh update of The Art of Building AI Coding Agents.

I released it early, before writing all the advanced material still in my head: dynamic workflows, connectors, sub-agents and managing the swarm, gateways, a message board so agents can collaborate, local model support, a deep dive on artifacts, and a self-wielding capstone. There are several chapters I owe you. The free version will always be online and up to date.

I released this book right after a successful crossover, because that is when we should test the main idea of this agentic codebook: that the agent, Ensemble, can be auto-regenerated from an agent reading the book, and that the book can be auto-updated by the agent it built. This is an expensive loop, and I’m paying for it out of my own pocket. This book predates that very first iteration, and I hope it may be a useful part of history as we climb toward the singularity.
